I will now run you through the main changes of the substantive part of the report in subsection A. In para. 27, the reference to technology was removed, as not all rules are equally applicable, considering, for example, that there are rules concerning specific weapon systems that will not be relevant or applicable outside of that context. The former para 34 was removed. This para attracted a great deal of attention and went through numerous variations. I understand that the use of "shall" is unacceptable to some delegations as it implies treaty language. However, using more permissive language, such as "should", will be problematic as it risks watering down existing obligations. As such, I have decided to remove this para, acknowledging that this is something that may become part of future negotiations on a possible instrument. The new para 34 has been brought in line with existing CCW language, namely that of the preamble of the Convention, which, of course, all High Contracting Parties have already agreed to. Para 35, and it was then 36 in the past, so please bear that in mind, reflects the state of discussions during our exchanges yesterday evening. I understand that for many, this para is acceptable as it stands, but that concerns remain for some delegations. We will be able to address these concerns in our consideration. also bearing in mind that the power should be read in conjunction with what precedes and what follows it. In that regard, we have brought it in line with power 34 to ensure consistency, but also to ensure that the language of this power is understood as a standalone provision, even if its consideration must be made in the context of the text as a whole. The language in para 36 has been amended to follow more logically from para 35 and has been adjusted to strike a balance, taking into account arguments from all sides of the spectrum. I appeal to you to also look at it as such a compromise. This para holds value for many delegations and, much like what precedes and follows it, It's not the place where only the interest of individual delegations can be reflected. Para 37. I have decided to split this para for better comprehension. I heard from some delegations that the crux of this sub-para lies in its beginning. and I hope that setting it out as its own sub-para may give it that targeted focus. Nonetheless, I retained the remainder of the sub-para in a new sub-para, as this language remains an essential measure for many. Para 37 includes principally stylistic changes to bring it in line with the rest of the text, thus avoiding inconsistencies. Paragraph 37 is, in essence, in line with the language of the 2023 report, while adding the necessary clarification to make it operational. Paragraph 37D includes mainly stylistic changes, the term material is now used throughout the text to improve its technical clarity, as terminology such as "substantially" holds a certain level of unhelpful ambiguity. The language in paragraph 38 has been amended to address concerns over varying national obligations. The way it's now formulated should in consequence sufficiently address these concerns and hopefully make the sub-paras acceptable for all. Para 39 includes a small amendment to account for the fact that an understanding is difficult to ensure. Instead, what we do is ensure that it can be understood. While I understand that para. 39 contains terminology that some delegations see as not being agreed terms under IHL, nor as having a shared interpretation, it is nonetheless a para. that holds great importance for a large number of delegations. In an attempt to bridge those differences, I have amended the text to add further clarification on what is meant and required by these concepts in this particular context. Paras 45 and 46 have, again, been amended to better reflect varying national obligations under IHL. The language in para 47 has been adjusted to add clarity to what the para covers and, importantly, what it does not cover. Thank you, Mr. Chair. We thank you, your team at the ISU, for the intensive work undertaken to bridge the widely differing positions in this room. We will study the text carefully and consult further before expressing more definitive positions, but on a preliminary reading, many elements do not reflect the level of ambition Switzerland would have preferred. Nevertheless, after many years of work, this package must be considered in light of the diversity of legal, policy and operational perspectives represented in the room and of the compromises required to achieve consensus. From that perspective, we could see this text as a possible landing zone. We would strongly urge delegations to preserve its careful balance. Any further deletion or dilution of substantive elements would risk upsetting that balance and placing the package as a whole in jeopardy. From Switzerland's perspective, the present text already represents a minimum substantive basis required for moving forward. Three considerations will guide our detailed assessment. First, whether the text is legally sound and internally coherent and whether it faithfully preserves existing obligations under IHL without weakening, qualifying, or interpreting them. And in this regard, we may return at a later stage with certain technical adjustments necessary in our view to ensure legal clarity and consistency. Second, whether it retains the essential logic of the two-tier approach, with clear prohibitions of certain systems and effective regulations of others. Finally, whether the text provides a sufficiently robust basis for moving beyond our present deliberations to the next phase of work. At a preliminary reading, we think that the text does that, and we remain ready to engage constructively with you and all delegations to iron out possible remaining differences. But we really hope that this balance will remain and bring us forward. Thank you so much.
